title: Paramount+ Scottish Highland Drama ‘Laird’ Adds Ruaridh Mollica, Holliday Grainger, Peter Mullan, Corey Mylchreest and More (EXCLUSIVE)
description: “Laird,” the upcoming Paramount+ series set and shot in the Scottish Highlands and starring Kenneth Branagh and Peter Sarsgaard, has rounded out it
body:
“Laird,” the upcoming Paramount+ series set and shot in the Scottish Highlands and starring Kenneth Branagh and Peter Sarsgaard, has rounded out its cast. 

	Jennifer Ehle (“Contagion,” “Zero Dark Thirty”), Peter Mullan (“I Swear,” “Ozark”), Phia Saban (“House of the Dragon,” “The Last Kingdom”), Ruaridh Mollica (“Vision Quest,” “Isle of Man”), Holliday Grainger (“Peter Melrose,” “Strike”), Douglas Hodge (“Legends,” “Joker”), and Corey Mylchreest (“Queen Charlotte,” “Hostage”) have joined the show, now in production. 
	

	Created by Jez Butterworth (“MobLand,” “The Agency”), John-Henry Butterworth (“Nine Perfect Strangers,” “The Agency”) and Georgia Lee (“Destination, Mudtown”) and with Joe Wright (“Pride & Prejudice,” “Atonement”) set to direct the pilot, “Laird” is described as an “epic family saga.”


	The story follows a proud Scot and Laird of Castle Drummoch (Branagh) who defies a shadowy American billionaire (Peter Sarsgaard) hellbent on buying up the glens. Amidst family feuds, buried secrets and star-crossed romances, he remains determined to protect his ancestral lands from oligarchical land grabbing.

	The show is produced by Paramount Television Studios and 101 Studios. Branagh will executive produce alongside David C. Glasser, Jez Butterworth & John-Henry Butterworth, Wright, Ron Burkle, David Hutkin, Bob Yari, Charles Finch, and Keith Cox. 

	“At its heart, ‘Laird’ is about one man standing his ground against unchecked wealth and power,” said Jane Wiseman, head of Originals for Paramount+. “There’s something universally resonant about watching someone fight to protect what matters most, and with Kenneth Branagh leading the series, and an equally remarkable creative team, we can’t wait for audiences to root for the Laird of Castle Drummoch”
	

	The series will premiere globally exclusively on Paramount+.

schema.headline: Paramount+ Scottish Highland Drama ‘Laird’ Adds Ruaridh Mollica, Holliday Grainger, Peter Mullan, Corey Mylchreest and More (EXCLUSIVE)

title: With ’Scrubs’ and ’Ted Lasso,’ Bill Lawrence Shows How Much TV Has Changed — and How Much It’s Still the Same
description: When “Scrubs” returned in February with new episodes after 16 years, the first season of the reboot had just nine episodes compared to the 24-episod
body:
When “Scrubs” returned in February with new episodes after 16 years, the first season of the reboot had just nine episodes compared to the 24-episode seasons of its original run. 

	“It might have taken us 10 episodes [back then] to figure out what’s working and gelling,” Lawrence said in an interview following an onstage chat during Advertising Week New York on Oct. 6. “Now, there’s an emphasis to hook people f—ing fast or we’re doomed.” 
	

	Lawrence appeared with Rob Caruso, senior vice president of consumer products for The Trade Desk’s Ventura TV OS, to discuss the changes the TV industry has undergone over the past decade — and the changes it will undergo in the future to meet the demands of a fragmented audience. 


	Lawrence’s career reflects those seismic changes. Today, he is balancing a bevy of shows including “Shrinking,” “Bad Monkey” and “Ted Lasso” on Apple TV; “Rooster” on HBO; the “Scrubs” reboot; and “I Suck at Girls,” set to premiere at a later date on Netflix.

	The dynamic Lawrence mentioned — having a limited amount of time to hook an audience — coincides with the rise of streaming and other industry shifts that stemmed from it. Caruso noted that shows used to necessitate mass appeal “versus now where you can write very nuanced shows.” 

	“You have no idea how daunting it was when I was first in the network business where we had to come up with a show that appeals to everyone,” Lawrence added. “Then it shifted to, if you can come up with a niche show that appeals incredibly strongly to a small audience, that’s the difference.” 
	

	Today’s TV creators must hook a potentially smaller audience in a shorter amount of time. The broader ecosystem is tasked with making that economically viable, at a time when consumers are discovering content differently than ever before, while also watching TV in more ways than ever before. 

	The TV operating system is incredibly important in that regard. It’s often the front door to how viewers discover content, and has grown into an essential component of how advertisers target and reach their audiences. For Caruso, perfecting the OS means strengthening how value flows back to publishers and TV manufacturers. 

	In the streaming age, algorithms have grown incredibly sophisticated to address these intricacies. But Lawrence and Caruso both cautioned that today’s algorithms can also backfire by pushing content in ways that miss the mark. 

	“When you see something that feels truly personalized for you, you don’t necessarily notice it,” said Caruso. “It’s like a good ad. You don’t necessarily think of an ad as an ad when it’s entertaining, when it’s targeted. When it’s not, when it starts to be spammy, you tend to tune out and it usually has the adverse effect.” 

	“Personalized” is the million-dollar word. Whether it’s a niche show for a smaller audience or an ad that reaches the right viewer, the future of the TV ecosystem may depend on innovating in how it finds audiences, helps them discover new content, keeps them coming back and monetizes their engagement. 

	With that, streaming platforms seem to be embracing advertising more and more as a revenue source, with most major premium platforms offering ad plans in addition to subscription services; free, ad-supported streaming TV (FAST) services are also on the rise. 

	Lawrence is obviously no stranger to TV advertising. He shared on stage at Advertising Week N.Y. that he thinks about the show’s format as soon as the pitch phase, selling a series both on what it could be like on an ad-supported network or, by contrast, on a subscription-based streaming service. 

	That said, he added that he’s stopped thinking about whether audiences binge a show or watch weekly. 

	“‘Bad Monkey’ is a good example of a show that every episode would end on a cliffhanger, and if you’re in the writers’ room knowing that one-third of the audience waits to watch until the whole season is out, you start asking yourself if they’ll have the same experience [as watching weekly],” he said. “I used to get hung up about it, but I’ve decided to just write shows as if people aren’t watching them all in a row.”
	

	There’s no denying that streaming has helped give new life to older shows. Lawrence suggested that the “Scrubs” revival happened partly because fans rewatched the show and new audiences discovered it on streaming. 

	“Ted Lasso,” too, recently came back after a much shorter, three-year hiatus between the third and fourth seasons. But Lawrence stressed that in both cases, there had to be a story worth telling. 

	Ultimately, that’s the best way to hook an audience, right? In a fragmented TV landscape, the right story has to find the right viewers. The economics of TV have changed dramatically since “Scrubs” first aired, but one thing hasn’t: great stories bring people together and inspire the next generation of creators.

schema.headline: With ’Scrubs’ and ’Ted Lasso,’ Bill Lawrence Shows How Much TV Has Changed — and How Much It’s Still the Same

title: Bollywood Actor Imran Khan Heads to High Court to Fight Order to Leave India Over Election Protest
description: Imran Khan is preparing a court challenge to an order that gives the Bollywood actor until Oct. 28 to leave India, after he attended a demonstratio
body:
Imran Khan is preparing a court challenge to an order that gives the Bollywood actor until Oct. 28 to leave India, after he attended a demonstration demanding that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar step down.

	Khan, a Bollywood superstar and Aamir Khan‘s nephew, is an American national who lives in India on an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card. It was at his home in Mumbai’s Khar neighborhood that the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) delivered the notice, a police officer said.
	

	A petition calling the Leave India Notice “drastic” is expected to reach the Bombay High Court as early as Friday. Its central argument is that nothing in Indian law or the OCI regulations bars a cardholder from attending a protest. Zulfiquar Memon, Parvez Memon and Chirag Naik of MZM Legal LLP are handling the case.


	Police rounded up upwards of 400 people across Mumbai on Oct. 10, many of them at August Kranti Maidan, where demonstrators had gathered in solidarity with a Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest in Delhi. The Delhi agitation centers on allegations that voter lists were manipulated during the Special Intensive Revision exercise. According to police, nobody had sought permission for the Mumbai event, and Azad Maidan is the sole venue where the Bombay High Court permits protests in the city.

	Speaking to reporters before he was detained, Khan said he had no demands. “I am here as a citizen, as someone who lives in this city,” he said.

	Police also picked up his girlfriend, actor Lekha Washington, and his cousin Zayn Marie Khan. From inside the van, Khan shared an Instagram selfie captioned “Apparently I’m going for a drive.” He had also taken part in CJP’s July demonstrations.
	

	Gamdevi police have since filed a First Information Report listing Khan among the accused. Kirit Somaiya, a former MP from the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), took a complaint to the same station claiming that Khan’s presence at the protest broke the terms of his OCI status and visa, and police passed it on to the FRRO. Somaiya, who wants Khan arrested and deported and has accused him of “political extremism,” separately asked Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan on Oct. 13 for a Look Out Circular that would flag any attempt by Khan to exit India.

	No OCI rule addresses whether cardholders can protest, and stripping someone of OCI status is a separate process from a Leave India Notice. The Union Home Ministry has used that power before, revoking the OCI card of Kannada cinema actor Chetan A Kumar, also a U.S. citizen, over “anti-India activities.”

	Khan stepped back from acting after a run of films that included “Delhi Belly,” “Mere Brother Ki Dulhan” and “I Hate Luv Storys,” which followed his 2008 lead debut in the Aamir Khan-produced “Jaane Tu Ya Jaane Na.” He also directed the 2018 documentary short “Mission Mars: Keep Walking India.” He is due to make an acting comeback with “Adhure Hum Adhure Tum.”

schema.headline: Bollywood Actor Imran Khan Heads to High Court to Fight Order to Leave India Over Election Protest

title: ‘La Bola Negra’ Soundtrack Features New Music From Composer Raül Refree
description:
“La Bola Negra” soundtrack, featuring music by composer Raül Refree, is set to be released on Oct. 16 by Lakeshore Records.

	Taking its name from
body:
“La Bola Negra” soundtrack, featuring music by composer Raül Refree, is set to be released on Oct. 16 by Lakeshore Records.

	Taking its name from an unfinished play by Lorca and drawing on his writings and legacy, “La Bola Negra” is directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi better known as Los Javis. It stars Guitarricadelafuente, Miguel Bernardeau, Carlos González, Milo Quifes, Lola Dueñas, Penélope Cruz and Glenn Close. It spans three generations and pivotal moments in Spanish history. In 1932, Carlos (Quifes) longs to belong in a fractured Spain. In 1937, Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) finds connection across enemy lines. And in 2017, Alberto (González) uncovers a long-buried family secret that gives voice to truths the past tried to erase.
	

	When scoring Netflix’s “La Bola Negra,” Refree knew he wanted to pursue a timeless, orchestral and avant-garde sound.


	It’s an intense score that grows along with the film and with the different protagonists as their stories unfold. 

	Refree, who is one of Variety’s 10 artisans to watch, tied his instrumentation to the characters rather than the eras. “Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) plays the trumpet, so his scenes rely heavily on the brass section. Carlos (Milo Quifes) plays the piano, so his music features the piano alongside the string section. Finally, Alberto’s (González) story takes place in the present day, and because he is going through a personal crisis, his music relies much more on silence,” Refree says.

	As the film progresses and the paths of the three protagonists cross in one way or another, the timbres and instrumental approach also begin to blend. “Mira que nos acechan” is where all the concepts come together, carrying the meaning that we are all one.
	

	Listen to the first of two cues from the film’s score, exclusive to Variety, below.

	“En España Empieza a Amanecer”



	This scene begins abruptly with a hard cut and marks a crucial moment towards the end of the film. Refree says, “I wanted the music to have a strong impact, with the brass section playing severely loud, and in sharply cut clusters that intensify the shock of this unexpected turn of events.”It’s a scene where the prisoners are forced out of their rooms, taken to their cells, and are later executed. “I imagined this procession of frightened prisoners and violent soldiers through a rhythmic pattern played by the strings – loud, aggressive pizzicatos. I thought the wood creaking quality of the strings created a sense of unease, almost as if the music itself were giving voice to the prisoners’ fear as they are led to their deaths. At the same time, I used electronic sounds, almost like a distorted form of tinnitus, to convey the disorientation the prisoners experience after being abruptly woken up.”The final melody is a minuet that Sebastián plays on the trumpet earlier in the film. Refree says, “It is a childlike piece that, for me, becomes the central theme of the score – a reflection of the fear and fragility of the film’s characters.”

	“Enfermería”



	“This was one of the first pieces I composed for the film, and it remains one of my favourites. This is the scene where Sebastián first sees Rafael. It begins with a relaxed, beautiful musical landscape led by the horns, evoking a sense of everyday life and daylight in a military hospital during wartime. The staccato trumpets add a touch of understated, almost casual heroism, as if suggesting the ordinary routines of soldiers living through extraordinary circumstances.”

	As the scene unfolds, however, the music begins to empty out, giving way to darker, lower melodic textures. “The bass trombone gradually takes the lead, and the intensity builds as Sebastián becomes increasingly overwhelmed by the sight of this beautiful, and injured body,” he says. “Musically, everything grows wilder and more dissonant, reflecting his inability to control what he is feeling. His attention drifts towards intimate details – the bare armpit, the small hollow at the base of Rafael’s neck – and the music follows him into this increasingly private, almost obsessive fascination. What begins as a beautiful, peaceful morning at the front gradually transforms into an intense, almost concealed intimate desire for which Sebastián has no control.”

	The film opens in New York City and Los Angeles on Oct. 16 before expanding to additional theaters across the United States and Canada. Select theaters will present it in 35mm. “La Bola Negra” will debut on Netflix in the United States and Canada on Dec. 2.

schema.headline: ‘La Bola Negra’ Soundtrack Features New Music From Composer Raül Refree

title: ‘Love of Your Life’ Director Rachel Morrison on  Margaret Qualley’s ‘Wild Range,’ Confronting COVID-19 and Subverting Romantic Drama Expectations: ‘Finding Herself Is Enough’
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for “Love of Your Life,” now streaming on Prime Video. 

	When Rachel Morrison read the script for “Love
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for “Love of Your Life,” now streaming on Prime Video. 

	When Rachel Morrison read the script for “Love of Your Life,” it stuck with her. 

	Penned by “Nyad” writer Julia Cox, the story follows Maya, a 20-something emergency room nurse living in Boston without much family to call her own. When she meets the nerdy but charming Charlie, the two start building a life together — until tragedy during the COVID-19 pandemic causes it to fall apart. Maya runs away from her pain by traveling the world, first to Portugal and then to London and Japan, but an unexpected romance forces her to confront her past and realize that there may be more than one love of her life.
	

	Morrison, who has already had an illustrious career as a director of photography — she was the first woman to be nominated for the best cinematography Oscar for her work on 2017’s “Mudbound” — made her directorial debut two years ago with the sports drama “The Fire Inside.” For her follow-up, she’d been thinking about the intersection of love and loss. 


	“I obviously was drawn to the script, but didn’t immediately think, ‘This is my next project,'” Morrison tells Variety over Zoom. “It really was just, this is good writing and I want to talk about it with this writer.”

	Morrison and Cox really connected. “There was a deep sense of mutual respect, but also, for this script that was incredibly well received and jumped off the page, she was not precious about it,” Morrison says. “The more I sat with it, the more it sort of got under my skin.”

	The same was true for the film’s cast, an all-star ensemble led by Margaret Qualley as Maya and including Gabriel Basso as Charlie; Aaron Pierre as Felix, a handsome stranger she meets abroad; Patrick Schwarzenegger as her best friend Jason; and Catherine Keener in a scene-stealing performance as Charlie’s mother Ruth. 
	

	“We have leading actors playing supporting roles, and I think that’s because this really spoke to them,” Morrison says. 

	Below, the director speaks more with Variety about working with Qualley, putting the COVID-19 pandemic on screen and why they didn’t go with the obvious ending. 
	
		What was it about the script that struck you?	

	I think there were two prominent things. One is that it’s sadly rare to have features where particularly female characters are layered and complex and flawed and messy and aren’t sort of reduced to just a plot engine, but actually have a lot of nuance and growth to do within the script. And I thought that was really exciting to see a character who could make some really questionable decisions, but you’re still rooting for her. 

	And then I think the reason why I was interested in the cross-section between love and loss is because of how personal it is to me. I’m somebody who was shaped from some pretty significant early loss that really transformed who I became. And I went through the same kind of messy tumult that Maya’s character did, where you’re trying to make sense of your life after something so devastating, and you’re moving through the world without actually engaging in it. These guardrails come up because you don’t ever want to be hurt again, and it’s a real process to take those down. So I think I saw myself in Maya and in the script, and felt like I could be additive to it. The more I sat with it, the more I realized how personal it was and therefore how right I would be to tell it.
	
		Tell me about finding your leading lady in Margaret Qualley.	

	Margaret had read the script — I mean, many actresses had read the script and kind of raised their hand. A few names stood out, Margaret’s in particular, where I knew she could be a real ally and partner in this. As somebody who’s going to have to anchor the entire thing, it’s critical that your actress wants to be there and really understands the film that you’re trying to make. We sat down and really talked about it, and it was clear we both wanted to make the same film. I’ve been a big fan of hers for a long time, and part of what I’m a fan of is this wild range she has. Her character choices are sometimes from one thing to the next, just these really bold characters. And I was excited that I don’t feel like in a feature sense, I’ve seen — maybe on “Maid” on TV — a really foot-on-the-ground, relatable performance that I knew she was capable of. And I was excited to see what the girl-next-door version could be.
	
	
		How about the men in Maya’s life: Gabriel Basso, Aaron Pierre and Patrick Schwarzenegger?	

	The biggest goal was for there to be variation between them. Each character had specificity as scripted, and actually as we cast the roles, they started to inform each other. Aaron is maybe a little more stoic than his character is written, which then allowed Gabe [to have] this kinetic, golden retriever energy. And then, obviously, doing chemistry reads with Margaret and Patrick too, and making sure that each of their chemistry was palpable but unique unto itself. And certainly Gabe brought out a different quality in Margaret than Aaron did and Patrick did, and you can feel it throughout the film.
	
		How has your career as a cinematographer informed your directing style?	

	First and foremost was the desire to shoot on real locations. People have different methodologies, but for me it was almost a non-starter. I really wanted to go to the spaces where this film existed, and not try to create them in a soundstage. And there are other directors who probably would skew towards the soundstage version, and so I commend Amazon MGM for actually letting me do it that way, because that’s not really how movies get made anymore. It’s actually really unusual to go to two cities, let alone four. 

	And then, I can’t turn off the DP in me, which I think is actually a real asset to my cinematographers because I’m scouting from the beginning. Even before the DP comes on, I’m looking at how the location interacts with light, how I can block a scene within a space to move the camera in such a way. So it’s sort of ingrained in how I visualize things, even probably from the page. And then [cinematographer] Todd [Banhazi], we had such a lovely collaboration. He’s amazing. But he kind of would light the world and then let me exist, which is how I like to work.



	

					Margaret Qualley and Gabriel Basso in “Love of Your Life.”
									©MGM/Courtesy Everett Collection
	


	
		The COVID-19 pandemic is a central part of the story. How did you go about portraying that and addressing our collective trauma from it, given that it wasn’t that long ago? Not many films have attempted to put it on screen.	

	I think for us, the most important thing was to get it right. Because this isn’t just the pandemic, it’s the pandemic as experienced through a first responder. And so we did a lot of consulting, both myself and Margaret, with nurses and doctors and just the medical profession during that time and the different stages of it. And then the lasting effects of it, of course. But I think just looking for little things that we would all relate to, even like “Tiger King,” wiping down the groceries with Clorox. The goal was really to recreate it in a way that feels both like yesterday and also like a lifetime ago, but that everyone would fully relate to. And not make it sensationalized. I think that’s the thing about the whole movie — I’m always trying to make it the grounded, relatable version of itself and not the cinema version of itself. So it’s never the extreme, it’s always the recognizable.
	
	
		Margaret has some very heavy emotional scenes. How did you work together to get her to that place?	

	Margaret had really great instincts. You have this character who spends a lot of the movie not actively grieving — it’s manifesting in these other ways, but she’s not actually releasing the emotion. Obviously, she’s feeling all the things and is traumatized, but she doesn’t quite know how to express it. On the day, there are things that happen always with good actors where they’re feeling the feel and there’s a reaction that isn’t even performative, it’s so from the body and the heart and the soul. So like, Margaret heaving trying to get the words out to Ruth on the phone, it was actually scripted that she got it all out and then lost it — but she couldn’t find the words. And I think she was right. It was a much more honest portrayal of what Maya would have been going through. I think my approach is you go in with a plan, but you’re always looking to pivot or react to what’s in front of you and not what you’d imagine. You have to be open to that, otherwise I think you can really stifle the process.
	
		At the end of the film when Maya flees the airport, I expected her to run back to Jason, but she actually goes to visit Ruth. Tell me about the decision for her not to end up with him.	

	You just touched on the other thing that drew me to this script, which is that we’re taking these genres that have a set of expectations and completely subverting them. It was very much by design that the audience thinks she’s going back to Jason for a moment, and then realizes she’s going to Ruth. And that’s because this genre is set up for the happily ever after romantic ending. And I am just so profoundly grateful and thrilled that that’s not how this film ends and that it really is so much more about finding her way back to life and to herself. The hope is now she will be open to all the possibilities in front of her — and will probably find the right person again someday and maybe still have kids and all the things — but we’re not spelling it out or buttoning it up for people and know that just finding herself is enough. 



	

					Aaron Pierre and Margaret Qualley in “Love of Your Life.”
									©MGM/Courtesy Everett Collection
	


	
		“Love of Your Life” got a one-week theatrical release before dropping on Prime. Why was this important for you?	

	I mean, I’m somebody that came from a time when dramas were in theaters. I made this film knowing it was always destined for Prime, [but] I made it for the theatrical experience anyway. I don’t know that I would ever shoot something differently because of the platform, but I’ve definitely been encouraging anyone and everyone to see it in theaters while they can because I do think there’s something so immersive about that experience for a number of reasons. There’s something very special about an engaged audience sharing an emotional experience together too, which is something that we just don’t get that much anymore because most movies in theaters these days are horror or action. The idea of all having a good cry together is quite rare. But, thankfully, I think it plays very well on Prime, too. And one thing that we learned just through the testing process is that — shocker — men feel more comfortable emoting at home. And so, it may actually play better for the male gender to just, in the comfort and privacy of their own home, really let it go.
	
	
		Any idea what your next film will be?	

	I’m interested in grounded sci-fi. I’m always looking for a device to hide the drama because I do want to make movies for the theater if possible. Because unless you’re Nolan or now maybe Coogler, we can’t get audiences to dramas anymore. I mean, even when you look at most of these films, like an “Arrival” or a “Blade Runner” or “Dune,” often they’re just simple [stories]. “Star Wars” is a father-son story, but it exists in space and therefore people are excited to go to the theater for the spectacle of it. So one bucket would be a big, world-building spectacle-y sci-fi drama. And I guess there’s another version where I make something smaller in the A24/Neon space where, by virtue of not making it for as much money, it gets a theatrical release because it can exist in a smaller space. But my goal right now would be to do something that’s undeniably theatrical and to do something that I haven’t done before. I’m always trying to push myself and challenge myself, hence the pivot from cinematography at the top of my game to starting completely over as a director. It’s to keep growing and evolving. So whatever’s least expected of me, that’s probably what I’ll do next.

	This interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity.

schema.headline: ‘Love of Your Life’ Director Rachel Morrison on  Margaret Qualley’s ‘Wild Range,’ Confronting COVID-19 and Subverting Romantic Drama Expectations: ‘Finding Herself Is Enough’

title: Guillermo del Toro Pays Tribute to Late ‘E.T.’ Designer Carlo Rambaldi Ahead of Hollywood Walk of Fame Honor: ‘A Worldwide Maestro of Magic’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Guillermo del Toro is paying tribute to Italian special effects master Carlo Rambaldi, who is being honored today with a posthumous Hollywood Walk
body:
Guillermo del Toro is paying tribute to Italian special effects master Carlo Rambaldi, who is being honored today with a posthumous Hollywood Walk of Fame star.

	Rambaldi, best known for designing the iconic title character in Steven Spielberg’s “E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial,” died in 2012 at age 86. He was a three-time Academy Award winner for his work in special effects, having won Oscars for “King Kong” (1976), “Alien” (1979) and “E.T” (1983).
	

	Prior to “E.T.,” Rambaldi had already collaborated with Spielberg on “Close Encounters of the Third Kind.” He subsequently worked with David Lynch on the cult classic “Dune.” The long list of top directors whom Rambaldi worked with over the course of his glorious career include Federico Fellini, Luchino Visconti, Pier Paolo Pasolini, Marco Ferreri, Mario Bava, Dario Argento, Lucio Fulci, John Huston, Ridley Scott and Oliver Stone.


	Rambaldi was born in the village of Vigarano Mainarda, outside the city of Ferrara, in the northern Italian region of Emilia-Romagna. The son of a bicycle mechanic, he graduated from the Academy of Fine Arts in Bologna in 1951 and, though he dreamed of becoming an artist, was drawn into the world of cinema when he was asked to create a dragon for a low-budget science fiction movie in 1956.

	Del Toro has been known to share a deep passion with Rambaldi for creatures used in contemporary fantasy and horror cinema made through the artisanal use of animatronics. 

	“Carlo Rambaldi changed the world of special effects, makeup and puppetry,” del Toro says in a video message shared exclusively with Variety. “He brought a know-how and a finesse and a great sense of character and design that can only be described as being the heir of the old world craftsmanship and beauty that comes with a country with a great theatrical tradition and a great artistic tradition.”
	

	Del Toro added: “Without him, it’s absolutely impossible to imagine the daring, beautiful work that is being done now and in the last few decades. He is not only a great Italian effect master, but a worldwide maestro of magic.”

	As previously announced, Rambaldi’s Walk of Fame ceremony is taking place on Thursday at 1611 Vine Street in Hollywood, attended by Cinecittà studios president Antonio Saccone, several of Rambaldi’s family members and Matt Winston, son of Stan Winston, the Oscar-winning special effects master who designed the dinosaurs for “Jurassic Park.”

schema.headline: Guillermo del Toro Pays Tribute to Late ‘E.T.’ Designer Carlo Rambaldi Ahead of Hollywood Walk of Fame Honor: ‘A Worldwide Maestro of Magic’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Sheriff Country’ Hits Series High of 5.5 Million Viewers as CBS Wins Premiere Week With Eight of the Top 10 Broadcast Shows
description:
CBS was the most-watched broadcaster of the week of Oct. 4-10, during which it debuted new seasons of the shows on its primetime lineup.

	The Eye
body:
CBS was the most-watched broadcaster of the week of Oct. 4-10, during which it debuted new seasons of the shows on its primetime lineup.

	The Eye network averaged 4.4 million viewers in primetime during that window, a significant lead on its next closest competitor, which was NBC with a 3.4 million-viewer average. ABC and Fox trailed with 2.6 million and 1.4 million viewers, respectively. 


	In addition, CBS was the only network to show growth compared to the same week last year, up 9% from last year’s 4.1 million viewers. It should be noted, though, that CBS did a heavier premiere-week push than its competitors, which premiered some of their shows in September and will debut others later in the fall.
	

	Among the highlights of CBS’ premiere week performance was “Sheriff Country,” the “Fire Country” spinoff that achieved a series high of just under 5.5 million viewers with its Season 2 premiere on Friday, marking a 25% increase on the Season 1 premiere last year. Also impressive was new drama series “Cupertino,” which beat “Law & Order” in the same timeslot with 3.2 million viewers. 


	CBS had eight of the top 10 broadcast shows from Oct. 4-10: “60 Minutes” with 10.2 million viewers, “Marshals” with 8.2 million, “Tracker” with 7 million, “NCIS” with 6.4 million, “NCIS: New York” with 5.6 million, “FBI” with 5.5 million, “Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage” with just under 5.5 million and “Sheriff Country” slightly behind “Georgie & Mandy.” The only non-CBS series to make the top 10 for the week were “Dancing With the Stars” at No. 4 with 6.4 million viewers on ABC and “Chicago Med” at No. 6 with 5.6 million viewers on NBC.
	

	Along with making the top 10, “NCIS: New York” and “Georgie & Mandy” were the most-watched new broadcast series and the most-watched broadcast comedy, respectively. 



	

	



	CBS showed year-over-year growth all five nights of the week. On Sunday, the network saw a 48% increase compared to last year, led by “60 Minutes” and “Marshals.” The Monday night lineup scored a 19% increase, with “FBI” in particular debuting with 24% more viewers than the year before. Tuesday —aka “NCIS” night — was up 40%, while Wednesday was up 8%, Thursday was up 14% and Friday was up 5%.

            Diddy busted his head during a fight with another famous, or infamous, inmate ... a Jamaican drug lord known as "Dudus," and TMZ has learned the fight was over Diddy getting all the inmates in trouble.
      
    
            Multiple sources inside Fort Dix FCI tell us ... Diddy and "Dudus" -- real name Christopher Coke -- came to blows last Friday, and Diddy got the worst of it ... suffering a head injury so severe, prison officials rushed him to an outside facility for treatment.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            We're told the two men were fighting because Dudus, and many other inmates, are pissed at Diddy for getting exposed in that NBC News report about his luxurious life behind bars. As a result, prison officials have conducted at least 2 raids and confiscated cell phones from inmates ... including Dudus.
      

            Now, while Diddy is clearly the biggest celebrity at Fort Dix, our sources describe Dudus -- who's been serving a 23-year sentence since 2012 -- as the real kingpin, and he's none too pleased all his fringe benefits vanished after the raids.
      
    
            We're told after the fight ... both men were placed in the Special Housing Unit -- aka solitary confinement -- for 2 weeks' punishment. To be clear, Diddy was already in the SHU due to the NBC report, and the fight went down when he was out for his daily break.
      
    
            TMZ broke the story ... Diddy was rushed out of prison by ambulance early Saturday morning to get emergency treatment for a head injury.
